qs.q: What is the primary hemodynamic consequence during ventricular systole in a patient with mitral regurgitation?
o: Flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium
Obstruction of blood flow into the aorta
Backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle
Restriction of blood filling into the left ventricle
qs.e: Mitral regurgitation involves incompetency of the mitral valve causing abnormal flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole. Obstruction of blood flow from the left ventricle into the aorta describes aortic stenosis.

qs.q: How does acute mitral regurgitation typically differ from chronic mitral regurgitation in its initial presentation?
o: Acute causes a rapid rise in left atrial pressure and marked symptomatic deterioration
Chronic presents with sudden onset acute pulmonary oedema due to normal compliance
Acute results in gradual left atrial dilatation with only a minor increase in pressure
Chronic immediately causes right heart failure with prominent ascites and edema
qs.e: Acute mitral regurgitation features a rapid rise in left atrial pressure because compliance is normal, leading to marked symptomatic deterioration. Chronic regurgitation involves gradual left atrial dilatation with minor pressure increases and few initial symptoms.

qs.q: Which of the following conditions is classified as a primary cause of mitral regurgitation?
o: Mitral valve prolapse
Coronary artery disease
Dilated cardiomyopathy
Myocardial infarction
qs.e: Primary causes of mitral regurgitation include mitral valve prolapse and rheumatic fever. Dilated cardiomyopathy and myocardial infarction cause secondary mitral regurgitation due to ventricular or annular changes.

qs.q: Which clinical sign is characteristic of moderate to severe chronic mitral regurgitation upon auscultation?
o: An apical pansystolic murmur radiating into the axilla
A slow-rising, delayed arterial carotid pulse
A diminished or delayed second heart sound
An early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge
qs.e: Moderate to severe mitral regurgitation causes an apical pansystolic murmur that radiates into the axilla and may have a thrill. A delayed carotid pulse is a sign of aortic stenosis rather than mitral regurgitation.

qs.q: What is the primary utility of cardiac catheterization performed prior to surgery in patients with mitral regurgitation?
o: To determine whether coexisting coronary artery disease is present
To measure the exact normal aortic valve circumference
To quantify the precise myxomatous degenerative changes in leaflets
To replace the need for an echocardiogram in left atrial size
qs.e: Cardiac catheterization before surgery is mainly done to determine whether coexisting coronary artery disease is present. Echocardiography is primarily used for structural and functional assessment of the valves and chambers.

qs.q: What is a standard component of medical management for a patient with mitral regurgitation and coexisting hypertension?
o: Vasodilators such as ACE inhibitors to reduce high afterload
Beta blockers administered exclusively to prevent chordal rupture
High-dose systemic vasoconstrictors to increase forward output
Immediate surgical annuloplasty ring placement without trial
qs.e: High afterload may worsen the degree of regurgitation, so hypertension in mitral regurgitation should be treated with vasodilators such as ACE inhibitors. Vasoconstrictors would increase afterload and worsen regurgitant volume.

qs.q: What is recognized as the most common etiology of mitral regurgitation in contemporary clinical practice?
o: Rheumatic heart disease
Ischemia / Myocardial Infarction
Congenital malformation
Bacterial endocarditis
qs.e: Mitral regurgitation is most commonly caused by ischemia affecting the papillary muscles, and nowadays it is more common than mitral stenosis. Rheumatic heart disease remains the overwhelming cause of mitral stenosis.

qs.q: During the pathophysiology of chronic mitral regurgitation, how is afterload affected as the left ventricle empties part of its contents backward?
o: Afterload is markedly increased because of pulmonary congestion
Afterload is decreased as blood enters the relatively low-pressure left atrium
Afterload remains completely unchanged regardless of regurgitant volume
Afterload is increased secondary to compensatory aortic constriction
qs.e: Afterload is decreased as the left ventricle empties part of its contents into the relatively low-pressure left atrium, which helps compensate by augmenting the ejection fraction. This volume overload eventually leads to ventricular dysfunction after prolonged periods.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Mitral regurgitation is a backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole, often due to valve prolapse, rheumatic disease or papillary muscle rupture. It leads to volume overload, atrial enlargement and eventually heart failure if untreated.

sections.p: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is incomplete closure of the mitral valve during systole, allowing blood to leak from the left ventricle (LV) back into the left atrium (LA). Diagnosis relies on a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, confirmed by echocardiography.

t.b: Shows regurgitant jet, valve morphology, LV size and function; a jet >50% of LV area suggests severe MR.
Peak velocity >3 m/s indicates severe MR; lower values suggest mild to moderate.
Enlarged cardiac silhouette and pulmonary vascular congestion point to chronic volume overload.

sections.p: Severity is graded by regurgitant fraction and LV dimensions. The American Society of Echocardiography uses mild (≤30%), moderate (31–50%) and severe (>50%).

t.b: Quantifies volume of blood leaking; >50% indicates severe MR.
LV dilation >55 mm suggests chronic overload.

sections.p: The leading causes vary by region: rheumatic fever in low‑resource settings, degenerative mitral valve prolapse in developed areas, and papillary muscle rupture after myocardial infarction. Other contributors include dilated cardiomyopathy, infective endocarditis, and congenital anomalies.

t.b: Identifies structural lesions (e.g., leaflet thickening, flail segment).
Rule out infective endocarditis if fever or embolic signs present.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, palpitations, and a new holosystolic murmur. In severe cases, a gallop rhythm and tender hepatomegaly may appear.

t.b: Detects murmur, gallop, and signs of right‑sided congestion.
Shows atrial enlargement or arrhythmias secondary to LA dilation.

sections.p: Echocardiography is the cornerstone. When unavailable, a focused cardiac auscultation and chest X‑ray can guide urgency. Blood tests rule out infection or systemic disease.

t.b: Answers whether MR is primary or secondary, its severity, and LV function.
Shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion, suggesting chronic MR.
Identify infective endocarditis if fever or emboli are present.

sections.p: Urgent red flags include acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, new atrial fibrillation, or embolic events. Complications of chronic MR are atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and infective endocarditis.

t.b: Detects sudden dyspnea or hypotension indicating acute decompensation.
New atrial fibrillation suggests LA enlargement.

faq.a: Yes, many patients have mild MR without symptoms until volume overload progresses.

faq.q: What is the role of beta‑blockers in MR?
faq.a: They reduce heart rate, lower myocardial oxygen demand, and improve LV filling time.
Severe MR with symptoms, LV dysfunction, or atrial fibrillation unresponsive to medical therapy.
